With card errata, rules changes, and the like? Let me digress first.

KoT will see reprints of numerous cards, some of which could be
changed for power level reasons or whatever. And, we've already
gotten a spoiler for a card that hose other cards.

Taking the latter first, while my opinion doesn't mean jack as I don't
die on CCGs, they die on me, it's quite annoying to see V:TES going
down the hose specific plays path. Vessel's Blood Doll annihilating
effect is awful. Then, we get Mary Anne Blaire. It's hard for me to
imagine that there won't be more either in KoT or later.

I'd guess the most likely nerfs in likely reprints would be the likes
of Freak Drive, Voter Cap, Parity Shift. Of those, the third seems
the least likely. If Heart of Nizchetus were reprinted in KoT, I
could see that. I tend to doubt seeing The Unmasking getting
reprinted, though there are various Cam allies that a precon could be
chock full of to where you could get Charisma and The Unmasking, which
should make for a highly valued precon. Just to tweak all of those
people who bitched about how gross the CE Ventrue precon was in
comparison to the others in terms of value, you could run Charisma,
Jake, and The Unmasking in the new Ventrue precon (along with the
obligatory "better than everyone else" stuff) for that one copy of
Political Ally and that one copy of Carlton Van Wyk while not putting
any of those cards in the Brujah Arms Dealer precon or the Tremere
Outcast Mage precon. That would be such a mindblowing FU that I'd
have to respect it.

The only reason to nerf something reprinted in KoT is if you decided
after KoT was ready for printing that something should be nerfed.
That seems kind of unlikely. So, I'd eliminate anything likely to see
reprinting. Leaving ...

1. Anthelios - Fred, the reason to nerf (actually, ban) Anthelios is
because recursion is often breakable in CCGs and because we've already
seen results that suggest Anthelios abuse. It's ridiculous to talk
about it being a symmetrical effect; throughout CCG history, players
have been breaking symmetrical effects. I have my doubts, though,
that anything will happen because there just aren't enough results
showing abuse.

In 2008, there's only wins for (numbers are attendance numbers): 21,
125, 144, 159, 12, 16, 12, 60, 15, 12, 18, 10, 32, 12, 10, 23, 12, 41,
19, 24, 11, 24, 14, 16, 22.

2. Heart of Nizchetus - Just as cheating doesn't always cause someone
to win, the official cheating phase doesn't always cause someone to
win either. My mind boggles at the existence of this card. In
theory, it could have added a built in steal effect a la The Erciyes
Fragments in an effort to make it less ridiculous. I wouldn't be
enthused as that's not likely to make it any less unfun. A more
desirable errata would be something like reducing it from 3 cards to
1. I give this an outside shot as it has shown up a lot in its short
existence.

3. The Unmasking - It's really good and all and ally decks are very
possibly stronger than they should be in a game about vampires even
ignoring the Imbued. But, it's not the end of the world when it comes
down. I'd give this a pretty low chance.

4. Direct Intervention - It might get reprinted in KoT, even more
likely if there's an intended nerf for the card, which would mean no
errata (barring misprintage). As I don't give a high chance of it
being reprinted in KoT, but I can imagine that something happening at
the NAC may be enough to push things over the edge, I'd give it an
outside chance. I still don't know, however, if the game improves by
nerfing it. Maybe it becomes more fun, which is a good enough reason,
but, as I said before, it theoretically serves a balancing purpose.

5. *shrug* - I'm sure there is some obvious card I'm forgetting that
either should get nerfed or has some significant probability.

Well, if there's a suspicious card in the decks that make the "best"
use of Anthelios, I would say it's Anson. Or Brother's Grimm, which
is actually awesome for ditching master cards quickly (you can discard
2 masters per MPA, oh and you get 5 pool eventually too). The
"problem", if there is one with Anethlios, is that you can effectively
use your ash heap as your hand, having access to anything there at any
point, without the chance of an action being blocked. In addition,
you can recurse any master card you want. There are a number of
master cards which get really good when you can recurse them as needed
without having to put a zillion of them in the deck. Vampiric Disease
is decent, IMHO. DI is good. Minion Taps, obviously. Stuff that can
be burned like Anarch Revolts and Smiling Jack. I know there are
several more that are really good with Anthelios, but I'm blanking
right now.

Now, I don't think it's a "problem", I just think it's good
deckbuilding when you take a strategy like the "mostly master card"
Anson deck, which is good but perhaps not great, and add a card like
Anthelios that just makes it better. You have to be set up to take
advantage of it, otherwise it is, like you say, just a no-cost Gehenna
card. But even a deck that isn't truly set up to take advantage of it
can still get some use out of someone else's Anthelios.

There is recursion in the game now, for better or worse (I think it's
better, but that's just me). Complaining about Anthelios *just*
because it allows recursion is not enough. Now saying that the type
or amount of recursion that it allows is too strong - well, I don't
agree, but it might be a valid argument, at least.

That said, if something does get banned or nerfed, I hope it's DI. I

> Besides, DI is the best defense against
> cards other people want to see banned, such as Voter Cap and Parity

I most respectfully disagree. Delaying Tactics is the best defence
against those cards. There is always a better, specific counter to many
of the basic threats in the game. DI is so good because it is a generic
counter. There are only 2 valid reasons I see for the existance of a
generic counter like DI: 1) to have a safeguard against overpowered
cards printed in future expansions until their power level is addressed
once the problem becomes visible, and 2) to give decks without access
to a good specific counter to one of the basic attack types a generic
counter.

I see the game is complex enough to be able to handle 1) more-or-less
effectively even without DI, and I see many good specific counters
being printed, e.g. Disengage, Lost in Translation, that can be used
in any deck.

However, DI is used by many decks and in practice it serves 4 purposes:
1) to stop other people from getting VPs long enough to move in for the
kill (this is somewhat similar to the seat-switching votes, although it
allows VP-sniping to a lesser degree); 2) to allow long "what-if-I-DI-
this" debates, effectively spending the game time, getting closer to the
time-out; 3) to hose high-yield, high opportunity cost cards, and 4) to
stop block fails cards in wall decks.

> Not every deck has bleed redirection or intercept. OBF/SER/PRE FoS decks
> come to mind. DI is good bleed defense for these decks (stop a
> Conditioning), when combined with Dummy Corporation and AI.

I have to disagree on this point. In every version of the OBF/SER/PRE
decks I played, I used DI to either prevent my prey from scoring a VP
or to prevent a card that would've killed one of my minions e.g. an
Immortal Grapple (I could've used Disengage for this but I'm anyway
playing DI to stop my prey from scoring a VP, so I might as well save
some overhead by exploiting its generic nature). As bleed defence I
used Dummy Corporation and Archon Investigation.

It makes no sense to use DI as a bleed defence. If you get bled for 2,
use Dummy Corporation; it is free. If you get bled for 3, which is
probably 1 base + 2 modifier, you are better off taking the bleed and
burning Dummy Corporation than DIing. If you get bled for 4+, you are
almost always better off paying 3 pool for the permanent bleed
reduction than 1 pool for the partial temporary one. :)

It does make sense to DI a bounce, but you have Narrow Minds now,
which is a very good card if you can play it early - it really wears
down the bouncers.

> Banning DI won't
> kill the game, but it will make playing decks without AUS or DOM/dom less
> fun (ie: get stuck behind a stealth bleeder and get ousted fast every
> time).

DI is no defence against a stealth bleeder unless you are a wall to begin
with. If you DI the bleed action, your predator will just play another
one. If you DI the stealth, your predator will just play another stealth.
If you DI the bleed modifier, you spent 1 MPA and 1 blood to save
yourself from losing 2-3 pool. Not bad, but Dummy Corporation or Archon
Investigation is better. In fact, if your grand predator is also a fast
deck, HE will DI the bleed mod that would oust you, so he can get 2 VPs
in a row.

Regards,

Daneel

You make some good points and, in general, I agree with you. Shear numbers
of appearances in the TWDA should not be considered evidence of undesirable
abuse/overuse of a card absent any other context. The question of whether
allowing a card to continue to be legal is a lot more complicated than just
looking at how often successful decks use it. Different kinds of cards are
intended for different roles, some rare, corner case, toolboxy in nature where
others are "staples", intended for and should be used in relatively large
numbers. Even amongst the former class, the one-or-two per deck kinds of
cards can be those which drop into any deck vs. those which only qualify
for a certain kind of deck archetype or are only usable with a given clan or
discipline. So you can't take anything from numbers alone.

On the other hand, I still think the TWDA can often be critical to sorting
out whether claims of abuse/overuse are valid or not. Too many times in
this newsgroup I see people making charges that a card is abusive without
any kind of evidence that its level of use in real life winning decks is
inappropriate for its intended role. Without such evidence, their claims
rest purely on their reckoning about the suspected card's upside without
really taking into account whether the same cards's various downsides are,
in fact, ultimately effective in preventing overuse or over-dependence on
the card to actually win. Without such evidence, they don't seem to
realize that it's impossible to prove that their hated bete noire is
overpowered; in fact, they've only demonstrated that they personally don't
care for the card's role. That's not the same thing as showing that a card
is overused in comparison to its intended role.

I suppose there could be other ways of proving the latter. I'm just not
sure what they are. Antecdotal evidence is pretty dicey.

Fred

Well, that's partially true. But I think the real reason that Voter
Cap is so good is that it's essentially Taste of Vitae and Street Cred
rolled into one card. Of course, Street Cred didn't exist at the
time. But take combat - as a strategy, it is much harder to oust your
prey with combat than it is with voting. You can build decks to take
advantage of either, but I still think that voting is more time-tested
as an ousting mechanism than anything having to do with combat. But
just assume they are equal in "power", whatever that means. Then, for
voting, you've got Voter Cap which gives you nearly unlimited blood,
plus up to 2 pool. Or, for combat, you've got Taste of Vitae which
can give you blood (though in practice, it seems easier to Voter Cap
for a ton of blood than it is to Taste for a ton of blood), and you've
got Street Cred that can give you up to 2 pool. (I tend to discount
the transfer acceleration because it also serves as pool gain
deceleration if you play it later in the game - for cards like Public
Trust and Street Cred, I feel like it mostly balances out - if there's
an advantage over "gain 2 pool", it's a situational one, and slight in
the general case.)

IMHO, Taste has proven to be a good card, and I think Street Cred is
on its way toward being proven good. And combat as a deck strategy is
certainly no *better*, or not *much* better at the very least, than
voting, right? That's why I think Voter Cap should at best be an
"either/or" situation.

It's just that causing (possibly massive) pool damage, gaining
(possibly massive) blood, *and* gaining pool all in one action is
incredibly strong. It's nearly at the point where a vote deck *must*
pack presence, because there is just no close alternative to Voter
Cap. It might be a solution to print a disciplineless alternative to
VC (maybe, "only usable when a vote passes, gain 2 blood"? 3 blood?
is that too weak?), but it seems clear to me that Voter Cap has always
been too strong, from the beginning. A slight nerf to superior to
make it simply "gain 2 pool" on a successful vote, means you have to
make a choice (although it could allow you to gain 2 pool on a vote
that only passes by 1), and would be ideal to me.

Leaving it as is and offering an alternative would be good, though not
quite as good IMHO, because it still leaves Voter Cap as clearly
overpowered, but perhaps you leave an overpowered VC and a slightly
weaker disciplineless alternative as cards that just happen to be
really good in voting decks and meanwhile continue to power up combat
decks through other means, like Dragonbound and Tension in the Ranks
have... It would at least power up non-presence voting decks (which I
still think are weak - I'm sure people can come up with a few contrary
examples, but in general, weak... I've seen the Amaravati Breed/Boon
decks, but I don't understand how those decks refill the 4 blood/turn
that Amaravati spends - I use Voter Cap in my version of the deck,
using Deviki Prasanta to get the skill cards...), without making
Presence voting any better.

Randomizing card effects/game results: Let's say you believe Blood
Doll is a better card than Vessel, so you only want to play BDs. In
one game, you face other like-minded players and no one's BDs
explode. In another game, you run into the Vessel crowd and your
blood management is toast. As long as you continue to play BDs, you
run into (everything else being equal in terms of how often you get
Suddened, Washed, et aled) extreme variance in card effectiveness.

So, since the point of good deck building is to weed out variance,
what are the answers? You can increase the number of Blood Dolls,
depend less on them, or stop playing them. The last can be ignored
for argument since done en masse means that BD is effectively banned
and somehow I doubt the playerbase is in favor of that. The other two
bring up whether it's fair and fun to punish someone who relies on
Blood Doll versus those who don't.

In terms of fairness, either the card deserves attacking or it
doesn't. If it does, then it's still going to be too good when the
hoser doesn't appear or, for whatever reason, doesn't work, which
means it's the card that should be fixed to avoid excessively swingy
results. If it doesn't deserve attacking, then there's a random
"punish someone for playing one specific balanced card" effect in the
game. Somehow, in terms of making CCGs more balanced, I don't
subscribe to the theory that going after fair cards is better than,
say, going after unfair cards.

In terms of fun, the "problem with counterspells" argument can be
brought up, only instead of generic counterspells that equally make
the game less fun, you have, essentially, a counterspell that unevenly
affects card choice. If you'd like a different comparison, then I
often compare the effect of having hosers in a game with the effect of
having combo decks in a game; either a combo deck does its thing and
the game suffers from its overpoweredness (if going off isn't
overpowered, then why bother playing a combo deck) or it falls flat
and the game suffers from having a nonfunctional deck at the table.
Hosers that have any impact - most don't - have a similar impact where
they either disproportionately nerf a card or strategy or fail to have
any meaningful effect, neither of which adds value to games I want to
play.

There's already plenty of randomness in V:TES. You have player
ability, deck choices, crypt draws for each player, library draws for
each player, mistakes, deals. Adding to these with having narrow
hosers only further randomizes play*, punishing the better deckbuilder
and/or the better player. It also punishes the segment of the CCG
playing audience who don't enjoy random effects, whether that's a
concern to others is debatable since it's hard to say how big that
segment is versus the segment who enjoy chaos.

* Or, the hoser is strong enough relative to what it hoses that what
it hoses ceases to see play. I believe that Vessel is good enough to
squeeze out BD in various places at various times as people decide it
isn't worth the risk of playing BD anymore.

Then, when you see more and more use of the hoser philosophy, you see
more and more randomness creep into the game to where it just becomes
painful to play. V:TES is nowhere near that and I don't hate Vessel,
in part because it becomes hard to care about how much CCGs get
screwed up, in part because I consider BD overpowered and even the
extreme case of effective banning only affects people who don't buy
new cards. However, I do fail to see how the BD killing effect makes
the game more enjoyable and I do worry that the hoser mentality will
expand until the game is as unpleasant to play as another one I can
think of.

bit and cost you a couple extra pool each game spent on Vessels but
on the whole, I would think that would smooth out much of the new
variance.

I've got the stealth bleed deck - which moves totally forward - and
you (again, my predator) have an animalism intercept deck. The variance
between those two situation is massive and will affect the table far
more than whether someone loses a few Blood Dolls or not. Again, I'm
not saying the Blood Dolls don't matter; only that your complaint

the draw-and-replace-to-maintain-hand-size kind of game that Jyhad is,
for which the flexibility of a card is by comparison far more critical.

instance. So you'd have to explain what you perceive is the "problem
with counterspells" argument and how it applies to Jyhad to be

that clearly targets a specific card or very small group of cards,
then perhaps I'd agree with that. But there's a lot of fuzziness in this
area - like the color hosers in Magic which, by contrast, affect many
cards in the game and, while often too narrow to make impact in a random
pick-up game or the first game of a match, can become critical sideboard
cards. In Jyhad, we have no sideboard and hence have never found a use
for, say, Letter From Vienna - if that's what you mean. But I see no
reason to take any overall conclusions about that situation which would
apply to Vessel. If that's what you're doing; I can't tell because
you speak in such generalized terms.

I think you're getting caught up in semantic traps:
1) Create a class of card in your mind - e.g. "hosers".
2) Make general conclusions about "hosers" based on what you've seen
them do in the past in Jyhad or in other card games.
3) Classify a new card, e.g. "Vessel" as a "hoser" based on certain
simlarities it shares with the class you've created.
4) Assume what's true for the class of card "hosers" is going to be
generally true of "Vessel".

I see people do this all too much. Such an approach to predicting
the effect of a new thing often tends to miss critical differences
between the new situation and former observations. I reject the
assertion that you can describe how Vessel affects Jyhad from
observations about prior hosers - in Jyhad or elsewhere.

Whereas I don't see people do this often enough. I consider it
fundamental to analysis to draw upon everything learned from prior
experience and observation and what can be gleaned from other people's
experiences and observations and try to formulate some sort of general
rule or philosophy. And, then, look for the flaws or exceptions as
further evidence comes in, not just take everything as unrelated to
everything else, where everything has a blank slate and the only way
to learn anything about something is to see what happens.

Fred, often you argue from the standpoint that you haven't seen
something that someone considers a problem, whether in games in LA or
wherever, and therefore, it's hard for you to believe there's a
problem. Up to a point, that's valid. But, no one player (or group)
is going to see or experience everything, which, BTW, is why there are
so many metagame differences. I don't believe that the entirety of
play is what I have firsthand knowledge of. To draw upon theory as a
starting point and then to try to draw upon every bit of thought that
can be found gives some hope of trying to understand everything about
a game.

Further, due to the complexity of CCGs, I believe it's essential to
make connections that involve theory in a way that I don't think you
find valid. To explain every underpinning for a belief is not
practically possible and would bore everybody to tears even if it
were, so you'll never get what you are looking for to question your
position.

Now, it's interesting when someone's experiences and observations
directly contradict my theory. It's certainly far more interesting
when the statistical evidence or the experiences and observations of
players at the higher competitive levels contradict my theory (when
it's a question of balance and not a question of fun). Theory is only
good so far as it holds up to testing.

Anyway, I'd be interested in which hosers you thought were good
additions to the game, but then, you'd argue that there shouldn't be a
class of cards termed hosers and we'd get as nowhere as we've gotten
so far.

accept until further evidence came in.

> Fred, often you argue from the standpoint that you haven't seen
> something that someone considers a problem, whether in games in LA or
> wherever, and therefore, it's hard for you to believe there's a
> problem. Up to a point, that's valid. But, no one player (or group)
> is going to see or experience everything, which, BTW, is why there are
> so many metagame differences. I don't believe that the entirety of
> play is what I have firsthand knowledge of. To draw upon theory as a
> starting point and then to try to draw upon every bit of thought that
> can be found gives some hope of trying to understand everything about
> a game.

Sure. That's fair enough. But are you going to ask WW to change the
card text of existing cards on that basis? I got the impression you
were. If you just want to discuss ideas about the nature of hosers, then
I'm fine listening to your theories. Of course, what I'd think was
interesting was how they related to Vessel and what evidence do have that
Vessel demonstrates what you're saying? Just me, I guess. I like to
pick apart details before I can really start believing in theories.

> Further, due to the complexity of CCGs, I believe it's essential to
> make connections that involve theory in a way that I don't think you
> find valid. To explain every underpinning for a belief is not
> practically possible and would bore everybody to tears even if it
> were, so you'll never get what you are looking for to question your
> position.

Your first sentence is a fair statement about me, indeed. The complexity
of CCGs is exactly why you can get into a ton of trouble trying to make
generalizations, in my opinion. And you can wring your hands about how
hard it is to communicate this but that doesn't alter the fact: details
matter! They matter a lot! (Well, at least some do...)

> Now, it's interesting when someone's experiences and observations
> directly contradict my theory. It's certainly far more interesting
> when the statistical evidence or the experiences and observations of
> players at the higher competitive levels contradict my theory (when
> it's a question of balance and not a question of fun). Theory is only
> good so far as it holds up to testing.
>
> Anyway, I'd be interested in which hosers you thought were good
> additions to the game, but then, you'd argue that there shouldn't be a
> class of cards termed hosers and we'd get as nowhere as we've gotten
> so far.

It's not so much that there shouldn't be a class of cards termed hosers.
It's just that you have to define what you're talking about. Semantics
are meaningless. You can define a class of cards and call them anything
you want, "hosers" or "blognoids" or "dkxrlk78bls" or whatever the hell
you want. Just as long as you give as much information about what you're
talking about as is needed for purposes of the discussion and it's a
useful definition for those purposes. I kind of think you didn't do that.
(But maybe I missed something. I often miss shit.)

As for what hosers I thought were good additions to the game, it depends
on the definition. If you meant things like clan hosers (Letter From Vienna),
very few if any at all. Clan hosers in this game have inevitably been too
narrow for the amount of good one gets from playing them. That's not a
necessary state of affairs. You could design one that was worthwhile with
the right technique. But it's always been true in the past.

But Vessel isn't a clan hoser so I don't think that can be what you meant.
We can talk about functional hosers (Unnatural Disaster, which hoses any
deck function that depends on a location) which can be quite good. But
the number of cards that can be seen as a "hoser", in that light, can be
much of the card population. Intercept "hoses" stealth; stealth "hoses"
intercept. Intercept "hoses" bleed. Bleed and combat "hose" pool gain. Pool
gain "hoses" bleed. I can go on and on. Direct Intervention and Sudden
Reversal hose damn near anything in the right situation. I honestly
didn't (and don't) know what borders you place around the concept of hosers.
The term tends to connote a card that applies to a very narrow situation and,
to balance its narrowness, either greatly rewards the player who uses it or
greatly punishes the player who was engaging in the function that got "hosed"
or both. (In a two-player game, of course, the punishment of one player and
the reward of his opponent are usually synonymous. In a multiplayer game,
they are distinct and the distinction can matter a great deal.) But how
narrow is narrow, exactly? The definition fuzzes and mutates, depending on
the context - a bad recipe for discussion, IMHO.

Fred

Nonsense. Not the way you completed it: with a _non_-generalization as
a caveat ("...not always a problem..."). Excellent!

Of course, as it happens I don't really agree with such a generalization
just because I don't, as a matter of experience. They can be problems at times.
Legacy of Pander was one I once thought was OK but have now been convinced
was probably reasonable to nerf, in retrospect. (Now that people have
won CQs with the nerfed version...) I was in lukewarm agreement with the
nerfing of Fifth Tradition when it happened. So I understand the potential
complaint with such cards. But most of those things above seem reasonable
enough to me. The exploitation of cards that offer open-ended rewards
takes precious time; the greater the reward sought, the more time it takes.
A well-designed card should make the cost in time balance the reward it
can potentially yield. As far as I know, the ones above seem to do that
pretty well. (Eldest Are Kholo, maybe, excepted. I haven't seen it used
to know.)

Fred
